glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 19 sets integrity above wealth and its fickle friends, finds wisdom in patience, a prudent wife, and timely correction, and places every human plan under the LORD’s counsel, while the false witness, the lazy man, and the scoffer reap what their ways deserve.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The sayings come from Solomon’s collection that begins at 10:1. Like 18:23, the chapter opens with the poor man, and repeated sayings about the false witness (19:5, 9) and the scoffer (19:25, 29) frame its first and last groups.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “There are many plans in a man’s heart, Nevertheless the LORD’s counsel—that will stand.” (Proverbs 19:21)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 19 opens with a comparison that defies the world’s way of keeping score: “Better is the poor who walks in his integrity Than one who is perverse in his lips, and is a fool” (19:1). “Wealth makes many friends” (19:4), while the poor man chases his friends “with words, yet they abandon him” (19:7). Twice the chapter warns that “A false witness will not go unpunished” (19:5, 9), and the second time the liar “shall perish.” Folly even turns on God, for a man twists his own way and then “his heart frets against the LORD” (19:3).

The middle sayings move into the home. Discretion makes a man “slow to anger,” and “his glory is to overlook a transgression” (19:11). A foolish son and a quarreling marriage wear a family down, but while houses and riches are inherited, a prudent wife is God’s gift (19:13–14). The LORD takes the poor man’s side so fully that pity shown him is a loan to God, “And He will pay back what he has given” (19:17).

Over every human scheme stands His purpose: “Nevertheless the LORD’s counsel—that will stand” (19:21). The fear of the LORD, a right view of God, “leads to life” (19:23), while the lazy man leaves his hand in the bowl and judgments wait for scoffers (19:24, 29).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 19:1–9 — Integrity, Fickle Friends, and the False Witness

A poor man who keeps his integrity outranks a fool with a crooked tongue, eager feet without knowledge run into sin, and the man who ruins his own way turns his anger on the LORD. Between two nearly identical warnings that the false witness will not escape, the sayings watch money gather friends and poverty scatter even brothers, and they call the getting of wisdom true love for one’s own soul.

Proverbs 19:10–14 — Discretion, the King’s Favor, and the Household

Comfort and power sit badly on those who lack the wisdom to use them, while a man of discretion shows his glory by letting an offense pass. The king’s anger and favor are set side by side, and then the household appears in both its griefs and its gifts: a foolish son and constant quarreling bring ruin, but a prudent wife comes from the LORD, beyond what any inheritance can supply.

Proverbs 19:15–21 — Pity for the Poor and the LORD’s Counsel

Idleness ends in hunger and carelessness in death, but the one who keeps the commandment guards his life, and kindness to the poor becomes a loan the LORD Himself promises to repay. Parents are urged to correct a son while correction can still turn him, the hot-tempered man is left to his consequences, and the call to receive counsel gives way to the LORD’s purpose, which outlasts every plan people make.

Proverbs 19:22–29 — The Fear of the LORD and Judgment for Scoffers

Kindness and honesty are what make a person worth having, and the fear of the LORD leads to a life of settled contentment. Against it stand the lazy man too idle to feed himself, the son who drives off his parents, the corrupt witness who mocks justice, and the scoffer, whose punishment teaches the simple and for whom judgments are already prepared.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 19 shows that God sees the people others walk away from. The poor man whose brothers hate him and whose friends desert him (19:7) is the one whose cause the LORD treats as His own (19:17). The repayment rests on God’s faithfulness and is no scheme for profit, just as 19:23 describes the general blessing of fearing Him without promising a life free of trouble.

The chapter also holds human effort and God’s rule together. The son is told to receive instruction, parents to correct a child while there is hope and never to aim at his harm, and the man of great wrath to bear his own consequences (19:18–20). Planning and counsel matter, yet only the LORD’s counsel is certain to stand (19:21). Wise people make their plans and then rest them on His purpose.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Integrity over wealth. A poor man who walks honestly is better than a fool with twisted speech or a liar, whatever either may own (19:1, 22).

Friends who follow money. Wealth and gifts draw a crowd, while poverty drives off even brothers; the sayings record this behavior without approving it (19:4, 6–7).

False witnesses. Lies told under oath will be answered, and the corrupt witness who scorns justice feeds on evil (19:5, 9, 28).

Griefs and gifts in the home. A foolish son, a quarrelsome marriage, and a son who shames his parents stand beside a prudent wife and correction given while there is hope (19:13–14, 18, 26).

Listening to counsel. Receiving instruction makes a person wise in his latter days, a rebuke teaches the one who understands, and the son who stops listening begins to stray (19:20, 25, 27).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Frets against the LORD (19:3). Raging at God over trouble a person’s own folly has caused. Scripture welcomes honest lament, as the Psalms show; this saying exposes the habit of blaming God for the results of one’s own choices.

Overlook a transgression (19:11). Choosing to let a personal offense go rather than nurse it or repay it. Overlooking an offense does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring sin that must be corrected.

Lends to the LORD (19:17). God counts kindness to the poor as done to Himself (compare 14:31; Matthew 25:40). The One who receives the loan is the One who repays it, so the giver’s confidence rests on His faithfulness.

The fear of the LORD (19:23). A right view of God, which means terror for those who defy Him and awe for everyone at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. Here it leads to life and to a settled satisfaction with Him, describing the general blessing of living in reverent trust.

The lazy man (19:15, 24). The NKJV speaks of “Laziness” and “an idle person” in 19:15 and “A lazy man” in 19:24. The man whose hand stays in the bowl uses biting humor to show a laziness that will not finish even feeding itself; the saying concerns unwillingness, not illness or inability.

The scoffer (19:25, 29). The one who will not be taught, because his problem lies in the will. Striking him may not change him, but the simple see it and grow wary, and the judgments prepared for scoffers show that contempt for correction meets correction in harder form.

1.brief: A poor man who walks with integrity is better off than a fool whose speech is twisted, whatever the fool may have. The comparison weighs character against advantage, and integrity wins even when it comes without wealth.
1.explain:
“Better is the poor who walks in his integrity”

The chapter opens with a comparison, and the first figure is a poor man. What sets him apart is that he “walks in his integrity.” Integrity is wholeness, a life that is the same inside and out, and “walks” makes it the steady course of his days. He may have little, but no loss of money can take this from him.

“Than one who is perverse in his lips, and is a fool.”

The reader might expect the other figure to be a rich man, and a near-twin saying does contrast the upright poor man with a crooked rich one: “Better is the poor who walks in his integrity Than one perverse in his ways, though he be rich” (28:6). Here the comparison is with a man who is “perverse in his lips,” whose speech is twisted and deceitful, and who “is a fool.” Whatever advantages the fool may have, the poor man of integrity is better off. The verse weighs character against advantage and finds character heavier. It does not make poverty itself a virtue. It says that honest wholeness before God is worth more than anything a crooked mouth can gain.

2.brief: Being without knowledge is not good for a person, and the one who rushes ahead with hasty feet sins by missing the way. Joined by Also to verse 1, the saying adds that eager energy needs understanding to guide it, or it carries a person into wrong before he has stopped to think.
2.explain:
“Also it is not good for a soul to be without knowledge,”

“Also” links this saying to 19:1 and adds another judgment of wisdom, this time stated directly: something is “not good.” A “soul” here is a person, especially in his desires and drives. To be “without knowledge” is to act on those desires without understanding. Energy, eagerness, and sincere zeal are not enough; desire that runs ahead of knowledge goes wrong. The line does not condemn desire. It warns against desire with no understanding to guide it.

“And he sins who hastens with his feet.”

The second line pictures a man in a hurry. He “hastens with his feet,” rushing ahead before he knows where he is going, and so “he sins.” The Hebrew verb behind “sins” is chata’, which can describe missing a target or missing the way, which fits the picture of hasty feet that miss the path. Yet the NKJV’s “sins” keeps the moral weight: rushing ahead without stopping to understand is not just a practical mistake. Haste that refuses to learn carries a person into wrong before he has stopped to think. Slowing down to understand is often an act of wisdom and faith.
2.notes:
The Hebrew verb rendered “sins,” chata’, is used in its basic sense of missing a target in Judges 20:16, where the slingers “could sling a stone at a hair’s breadth and not miss” (Judges 20:16). The ESV renders this line with the hasty man who ‘misses his way,’ and the AMP reads ‘sins (misses the mark),’ keeping both senses together.

The Hebrew word behind “soul” is nefesh, which can mean a person, a life, or a person’s appetite and desire. The ESV renders the first line ‘Desire without knowledge is not good,’ taking the word in that last sense, which fits the picture of eager feet that rush ahead.

3.brief: Through his own foolishness a man wrecks the course of his life, and then his heart rages against the LORD for what has happened. The saying exposes the folly of blaming God for trouble one has caused, which is different from the honest lament Scripture welcomes.
3.explain:
“The foolishness of a man twists his way,”

A man’s own “foolishness” is the cause here. It “twists his way,” wrecking or overturning the course of his life. The trouble that follows is not mysterious; it grows from his own choices. Proverbs consistently traces ruin back to folly rather than to blind fate.

“And his heart frets against the LORD.”

Then comes the strange turn. Having ruined his own way, the man’s “heart frets against the LORD.” He rages at God for the results of what he himself did. The cause is in the first line, and the anger is aimed in the second. The verse exposes the habit of blaming God for self-made trouble rather than owning it. This is different from the honest lament Scripture welcomes. The Psalms are full of believers pouring out pain, confusion, and questions before God, often in times when they had done nothing to cause their suffering. What this saying warns against is turning against the LORD over a ruin one’s own folly produced. The right response to such trouble is to own it and turn back to Him.

4.brief: Wealth attracts plenty of friends, while the poor man finds even his friend pulling away. The proverb states plainly how people tend to behave around money; it describes the world as it is without approving it.
4.explain:
“Wealth makes many friends,”

Money attracts people. “Wealth makes many friends,” or at least many people who act like friends. They gather around what the rich man has, and they enjoy what he can give them.

“But the poor is separated from his friend.”

The poor man has the opposite experience. Not only does he lack a crowd; he is “separated from his friend,” losing even the one companion he had. The two lines are a plain observation about how people tend to behave around money. The proverb describes the world as it is without approving it. Proverbs elsewhere condemns oppressing the poor and fawning over the rich, and this saying does not endorse favoring wealth. Its honesty protects the reader from naivety about the crowd that gathers around money, and it quietly exposes how shallow such friendships are. Proverbs made a similar observation earlier: “The poor man is hated even by his own neighbor, But the rich has many friends” (14:20). The theme returns in 19:6–7.

5.brief: The false witness will not escape punishment, and the one who breathes out lies will not get away. Courts may be fooled for a time, but this saying insists that perjury will be answered.
5.explain:
“A false witness will not go unpunished,”

The scene shifts to the court. A “false witness” gives untrue testimony against someone, a serious crime in Israel because a person’s property, freedom, or life could depend on the word of witnesses. The law commanded that a false witness receive the penalty he had tried to bring on his neighbor. The saying declares that such a person “will not go unpunished.” A court may be fooled for a time, but the matter is not finished.

“And he who speaks lies will not escape.”

The second line widens the warning to anyone who “speaks lies.” The liar often uses his lie as an escape, a way out of trouble or a way to gain an advantage. The verse turns that upside down: he “will not escape.” What he meant as a way out becomes a trap. This saying is repeated almost exactly in 19:9, and the two warnings enclose the sayings of 19:6–8 within the chapter’s opening section.
5.notes: The law set the penalty for a false witness: “then you shall do to him as he thought to have done to his brother” (Deuteronomy 19:19).

6.brief: Many people seek the favor of those in high places, and everyone wants to be friends with a man who gives gifts. Returning to the theme of verse 4, the saying observes how generosity and rank draw a crowd of hangers-on.
6.explain:
“Many entreat the favor of the nobility,”

Many people seek the favor of “the nobility,” those of high rank and influence. To “entreat the favor” is to court someone, to try to win his goodwill. People flock to the powerful because of what the powerful can do for them.

“And every man is a friend to one who gives gifts.”

The second line states the motive plainly. “Every man is a friend” to the person who gives gifts. Such friendship is commercial; it lasts as long as the gifts keep coming. Returning to the theme of 19:4, the saying observes how generosity and rank draw a crowd. It does not condemn generosity or deny that giving can build goodwill. It exposes how much friendship in the world is really attachment to what another person supplies. The next verse shows the other side, when the gifts stop.
6.notes:
The Hebrew phrase behind “entreat the favor” joins a verb meaning to soothe or entreat with the word for “face.” It describes seeking someone’s goodwill by appealing to him in person. The same expression is used of prayer: “I entreated Your favor with my whole heart” (Psalm 119:58).

The Hebrew word rendered “nobility” is nadib, which can describe a person who is noble in rank or noble and generous in character. The ESV and NASB read ‘a generous man,’ which connects the first line closely to the gift-giver of the second.

7.brief: Even the poor man’s own brothers turn against him, and his friends keep their distance all the more. He chases after them with pleading words, yet they are gone, a painful picture of how poverty can strip a person of support.
7.explain:
“All the brothers of the poor hate him;”

This verse is unusual in Proverbs because it has three lines instead of two. It begins with family. “All the brothers of the poor hate him.” “Hate” in Proverbs can mean to reject or turn away from someone, and here even his own relatives keep their distance. Poverty strips away the support a person would most expect to keep.

“How much more do his friends go far from him!”

If brothers, bound by blood, turn away, “how much more” will friends who have no such tie. They “go far from him,” putting distance between themselves and his need.

“He may pursue them with words, yet they abandon him.”

The third line shows the poor man still trying. He “may pursue them with words,” pleading, calling after them, asking for help, “yet they abandon him.” His words reach no one. This is one of the most painful pictures of loneliness in Proverbs. Like 19:4 and 19:6, it describes what happens without approving it, and it lets the reader feel the cost of poverty from the inside. God sees this loneliness and has written it into His Word, and His law repeatedly commands His people to open their hands to the poor rather than walk away from them.
7.notes: The third line is difficult in Hebrew. The written Hebrew text reads a word meaning “not,” while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has a word that sounds the same but means “to him.” Translations therefore differ. The NKJV describes the friends abandoning him, the ESV reads ‘but does not have them,’ the NASB and AMP ‘they are gone,’ and the YLT ‘they are not!’ Every reading leaves the poor man alone.

8.brief: Whoever gains wisdom shows love for his own life, and whoever holds on to understanding will find good. Seeking wisdom is not selfish in a wrong sense; it is the truest care a person can show for his own soul.
8.explain:
“He who gets wisdom loves his own soul;”

To get wisdom is to acquire it, as one would acquire a valuable possession. The person who does this “loves his own soul,” showing true care for his own life. Seeking wisdom is not selfish in a wrong sense, and it is not a burden laid on happiness. It is the deepest good a person can do for himself, because wisdom leads to life. The fool who refuses wisdom is in effect his own enemy.

“He who keeps understanding will find good.”

The second line moves from getting to keeping. It is not enough to acquire understanding once; a person must hold on to it, guard it, and live by it. The one who “keeps understanding will find good.” This is the general pattern of God’s ordered world: wisdom kept and practiced tends to bring good. Getting must become keeping, as the father urged elsewhere: “Take firm hold of instruction, do not let go; Keep her, for she is your life” (4:13).
8.notes: Where the NKJV has “He who gets wisdom,” the Hebrew words qoneh lev say literally ‘He who gets heart,’ so the whole first line reads ‘He who gets heart loves his own soul.’ The KJV margin notes that “wisdom” is literally ‘an heart,’ and the YLT reads ‘Whoso is getting heart is loving his soul.’ In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and judgment, not only of feeling, so to get a heart means to gain understanding. The expression is the opposite of the young man “devoid of understanding,” literally lacking heart, in 7:7.

9.brief: The warning of verse 5 returns almost word for word, except that now the liar will perish. The repetition frames the opening section and strengthens the sentence: deceit that harms others ends in the liar’s own ruin.
9.explain:
“A false witness will not go unpunished,”

The opening line of 19:5 returns word for word. The repetition is deliberate. Together with 19:5 it encloses the sayings of 19:6–8 within the chapter’s opening section, and it presses the warning home. When Proverbs says something twice, it wants the reader to be sure.

“And he who speaks lies shall perish.”

The second line changes one word. In 19:5 the liar “will not escape”; here he “shall perish.” The sentence grows heavier. The lie that harms others ends in the liar’s own ruin. Between the two sayings stand verses about the poor man abandoned by brothers and friends, the kind of person most vulnerable to false testimony. The frame suggests that God is especially watchful when lies are told against those who have no one to speak for them. The verse does not say how or when the liar will perish, but it is certain that he will not finally get away.

10.brief: Luxury does not suit a fool, and in the social order of Solomon’s day it was even more out of place for a servant to rule over princes. The point is the disorder that follows when comfort or power arrives without the wisdom to handle it, not a judgment on servants, for a wise servant can rightly rule (17:2).
10.explain:
“Luxury is not fitting for a fool,”

“Luxury” is comfort, delight, and plenty. It “is not fitting for a fool” because he lacks the wisdom to handle it. Comfort does not make a person; it reveals him, and in a fool’s hands it feeds his folly and makes him worse. Proverbs elsewhere lists “A fool when he is filled with food” among the things the earth cannot bear (30:22).

“Much less for a servant to rule over princes.”

“Much less” argues from the lesser to the greater. In the social order of Solomon’s day, a servant suddenly raised to rule over princes was an even greater disruption, especially when he came to power without preparation or character. Proverbs lists the same picture: “For a servant when he reigns” (30:22). The point is the disorder that follows when power arrives without the wisdom to use it. The verse passes no judgment on servants as such. Proverbs has already praised “A wise servant” who rules over a shameful son (17:2), and Scripture tells of Joseph, sold as a slave, who ruled Egypt well. The danger lies in the unprepared and unwise, whatever their station.

11.brief: Good sense makes a person slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. Patience and the willingness to let a personal wrong go are marks of wisdom, though overlooking an offense does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring sin that must be corrected.
11.explain:
“The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger,”

“Discretion” is good sense, insight into people and situations. It “makes him slow to anger.” The Hebrew says literally that it makes his anger long, giving it a long fuse. A person who understands more of what is happening, and why, has room to be patient. Quick anger usually reacts to the surface; discretion sees deeper and waits.

“And his glory is to overlook a transgression.”

The second line goes further. A man’s “glory,” his honor and beauty, is “to overlook a transgression,” to pass over an offense done against him rather than nurse it or repay it. The world often sees this as weakness. Proverbs calls it glory. In this, a person acts like God, who is praised as “Pardoning iniquity And passing over the transgression of the remnant of His heritage” (Micah 7:18). Overlooking a personal wrong does not mean tolerating abuse, ignoring harm done to others, or leaving sin uncorrected when correction is needed. It means choosing not to hold onto a personal slight, and it is a mark of wisdom and strength.
11.notes: The Hebrew phrase behind “overlook” is literally ‘pass over.’ Micah uses the same verb with the same word for “transgression” when he praises God for “passing over the transgression” (Micah 7:18), so the person who overlooks an offense is acting in a way Scripture also ascribes to God.

12.brief: The king’s anger is as fearsome as a roaring lion, but his favor is as refreshing as dew on the grass. Those who live under a ruler’s authority should take both seriously, since he holds the power to threaten or to bless.
12.explain:
“The king’s wrath is like the roaring of a lion,”

The roar of a lion is a fearsome sound, and the “king’s wrath” is like that roar. A king held the power of life and death, and his anger was dangerous to anyone who provoked it. Proverbs uses the same picture in 20:2: “The wrath of a king is like the roaring of a lion” (20:2).

“But his favor is like dew on the grass.”

The second line gives the opposite picture. The king’s “favor is like dew on the grass.” In a dry land, dew kept vegetation alive through rainless seasons, falling quietly and refreshing everything it touched. A king’s favor is like that: gentle, life-giving, and welcome. Those who live under a ruler’s authority are wise to take both seriously, avoiding what provokes his anger and valuing his favor. The saying also shows the weight carried by anyone in authority. Anger from above lands hard, and kindness from above refreshes.
12.notes: Proverbs describes royal favor with a similar image of moisture: “his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain” (16:15).

13.brief: A foolish son brings ruin on his father, and quarreling in a marriage is like a steady drip that never stops. Both lines describe pain inside the home, the second pointing to strife that wears down a household over time.
13.explain:
“A foolish son is the ruin of his father,”

The verse turns to pain inside the home. A “foolish son” is “the ruin of his father,” bringing calamity on him, whether through disgrace, wasted resources, or broken hopes. Proverbs is not sentimental about family life. It names the grief a wayward child can bring. Yet, as in 17:21 and 17:25, the saying describes the father’s loss without blaming him for his son’s choices.

“And the contentions of a wife are a continual dripping.”

The second line names another pain: “the contentions of a wife” are “a continual dripping,” like water dripping steadily through a leaking roof. One drop is nothing; endless drops wear on a person until he can find no rest. The picture is of strife that never stops, wearing down a household over time. This is a portrait of strife in a home, not a joke about wives, and the same truth applies to a quarrelsome husband. The verse shows how much the peace of a home depends on everyday words. Proverbs uses the same image in 27:15, and the very next verse in this chapter, 19:14, sets the prudent wife beside the contentious one.
13.notes: The image recurs in 27:15: “A continual dripping on a very rainy day And a contentious woman are alike” (27:15).

14.brief: A man may inherit houses and wealth from his father, but a wise and prudent wife comes from the LORD. Possessions can be passed down, while a good spouse is a gift only God can give, in contrast to the quarreling of verse 13.
14.explain:
“Houses and riches are an inheritance from fathers,”

Some things can be passed down. “Houses and riches” come as “an inheritance from fathers,” handed from one generation to the next. A man may receive property without doing anything to earn it, simply because of the family he was born into.

“But a prudent wife is from the LORD.”

Other gifts cannot be inherited. “A prudent wife,” one who is wise and discerning, “is from the LORD.” No father can bequeath her, and no amount of property can buy her character. She is a gift only God can give. The verse stands in contrast to the quarreling of 19:13 and echoes 18:22, which calls a wife “a good thing” and says the man who finds her “obtains favor from the LORD.” It points to God’s hand in the most personal parts of life. It is not a promise that every marriage will be easy, and it does not suggest that a hard marriage means God gave the wrong gift. It honors a wise spouse as one of the LORD’s best gifts.
14.notes: The Hebrew word behind “prudent” describes insight and good sense. It comes from the same root as the word used in 19:11 for the “discretion” that makes a man slow to anger, so the wife of 19:14 has the same quality of wise insight that 19:11 praises.

15.brief: Laziness drops a person into deep sleep, and the idle soul will go hungry. The lazy man’s drowsiness is not harmless rest, for it leads straight to want.
15.explain:
“Laziness casts one into a deep sleep,”

Laziness here acts on the person. It “casts one into a deep sleep,” pulling him down into a heavy drowsiness. The more a person gives in to slackness, the harder it is to wake up. What begins as a small indulgence becomes a weight. The “deep sleep” is not refreshing rest but dullness that settles over a life until a person no longer notices what needs doing.

“And an idle person will suffer hunger.”

The second line shows the result. “An idle person,” in Hebrew literally a slack soul, meaning a person whose will has gone limp, “will suffer hunger.” The lazy man’s drowsiness leads straight to want. He sleeps while work waits, and so there is nothing to eat. The verse addresses settled unwillingness to work. It does not condemn rest, which God gives as a good gift, and it does not describe those who cannot work because of illness, grief, exhaustion, or disability. Proverbs portrays the lazy man fully elsewhere; this saying shows the downward pull of laziness and its plain consequence.
15.notes: The Hebrew word for “deep sleep” is tardemah, a heavy sleep from which a person is not easily roused. It is the same word used when “the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam” (Genesis 2:21). The comparison concerns the depth of the sleep, not its source.

16.brief: Whoever keeps the commandment guards his own life, but the one who is careless about how he lives will die. Obedience to God’s instruction protects the soul, and indifference to one’s ways is deadly.
16.explain:
“He who keeps the commandment keeps his soul,”

The verb “keeps” appears twice. The one who keeps “the commandment,” God’s instruction, “keeps his soul,” guarding his own life. Obeying God is not a fence that hems in a person’s good; it is the wall that protects it. The “commandment” here may refer to God’s law or to the wise instruction that applies it, and in Proverbs the two run together.

“But he who is careless of his ways will die.”

The opposite is the one who is “careless of his ways,” who does not care how he lives or where his life is going. The Hebrew word behind “careless” means to despise or hold in contempt, and the KJV and ESV read “despises.” Not caring about one’s ways is a quiet way of despising them. Such a person “will die.” Indifference to the direction of life is deadly, while attention to God’s instruction protects it. As with other proverbs, this states the general pattern of God’s ordered world rather than a timetable for every life.

17.brief: Showing kindness to the poor is the same as lending to the LORD, and He will repay what was given. God counts mercy to the needy as done to Himself (compare Matthew 25:40), and the repayment rests on His faithfulness, not on a scheme for financial gain.
17.explain:
“He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD,”

To have “pity on the poor” is to show them grace and kindness, to give to their need. The Hebrew verb behind “has pity” means to be gracious or to show favor, and it is often used for God’s own graciousness. The striking claim is that such a person “lends to the LORD.” God counts kindness to the poor as a loan made to Himself. He identifies so closely with the needy that what is done for them is done for Him. Jesus taught the same: “inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me” (Matthew 25:40). Earlier, Proverbs said that oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker; here kindness to them reaches Him.

“And He will pay back what he has given.”

The LORD who receives the loan is the one who repays it. “He will pay back what he has given.” The giver need not look to the poor for repayment; God Himself takes responsibility for the debt. This rests on His faithfulness and character. It is not a scheme for financial gain or an investment plan that guarantees money in return. God repays in His own way and time, and His reward may come in many forms. The verse invites generosity by assuring the giver that no kindness to the poor is lost or forgotten before God.

18.brief: Parents are told to correct their son while there is still hope, during the years when correction can still turn him. They must never aim at the child’s ruin, whether by withholding needed discipline or by punishing in anger, and the verse gives no license for harshness or abuse.
18.explain:
“Chasten your son while there is hope,”

To “chasten” is to discipline, and in Proverbs discipline is the whole work of teaching, guiding, correcting, and training a child toward maturity. It includes correction and fitting consequences, but it is much broader than punishment. Proverbs has already said that loving parents do not neglect this work: “he who loves him disciplines him promptly” (13:24). This verse adds urgency. Discipline belongs to the time “while there is hope,” the years when a child is still teachable and correction can still turn him. Loving discipline is an act of hope. It says the child can still change, and it does the work now rather than giving up or waiting until it is too late. The verse does not guarantee how a child will turn out; it urges parents to use the season they have.

“And do not set your heart on his destruction.”

The second line sets a boundary, and its exact sense is debated. It may warn parents not to make themselves party to a child’s ruin by withholding needed discipline, leaving him to a path that ends in death. Or it may warn parents not to let correction become destructive, disciplining in anger or to the point of harm. On either reading, the parent’s aim must be the child’s life and good, never his ruin, and the verse gives no license for harshness, rage, or abuse. The New Testament keeps the same balance: “fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath, but bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Behind every parent stands the LORD Himself, who corrects His children because He loves them (3:12) and whose discipline aims at their holiness and “the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:11).
18.notes: Translations of the second line vary widely. The NKJV reads “do not set your heart on his destruction,” the ESV ‘do not set your heart on putting him to death,’ and the NASB (1995 edition) ‘do not desire his death.’ The KJV reads ‘let not thy soul spare for his crying,’ and its margin offers ‘to his destruction’ or ‘to cause him to die’ as alternatives. The Hebrew can be read as a warning against neglect or against excess, which is why both readings are given above.

19.brief: Great anger brings its own punishment on a man, and if you rescue him from the consequences, you will only have to do it again. Shielding a hot-tempered person from the results of his anger does not cure him.
19.explain:
“A man of great wrath will suffer punishment;”

A man of “great wrath” has a hot, uncontrolled temper. Such anger brings its own consequences; he “will suffer punishment,” paying a penalty for what his temper leads him to do. Quarrels, broken relationships, legal trouble, and harm to himself follow the angry man.

“For if you rescue him, you will have to do it again.”

The second line speaks to those around him. “If you rescue him,” shielding him from the consequences of his anger, “you will have to do it again.” Rescue without change only repeats the cycle: wrath, trouble, rescue, and wrath again. The saying does not forbid mercy or help. It observes that protecting a hot-tempered person from the results of his anger does not cure him, and that letting consequences teach can be part of love. Only a real change of heart breaks the pattern, and that change is something God must work. Wise boundaries are sometimes the kindest thing a person can offer.
19.notes: The KJV margin notes that “do it again” is literally ‘add,’ and the YLT reads ‘yet again thou dost add.’ In the first line the written Hebrew has a rare word meaning harsh or rough, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts is the common word for “great.” The NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV follow the marginal reading, “great wrath,” and either way the line describes a man whose anger is out of control.

20.brief: The father urges the son to listen to counsel and accept instruction now, so that he may be wise in the later years of his life. Teachability in youth produces wisdom that lasts into old age.
20.explain:
“Listen to counsel and receive instruction,”

The father speaks directly. “Listen to counsel,” advice from those who know more, “and receive instruction,” accepting teaching and correction. The two commands require humility, the willingness to admit that one does not already know everything. In a section that has just spoken of chastening a son, this verse addresses the son himself and calls him to welcome what he is taught.

“That you may be wise in your latter days.”

The goal reaches far ahead: “That you may be wise in your latter days,” in the later years of life. The counsel accepted today shapes who a person will be at the end. Teachability in youth produces wisdom that lasts into old age. Even great wisdom must be kept by continued listening. Solomon himself, the wisest of men, turned aside when he was old, as 1 Kings 11:4 records. The verse pairs naturally with 19:21. A person should seek and receive counsel in making plans, while knowing that the LORD’s counsel has the final word.

21.brief: People make many plans in their hearts, but it is the LORD’s purpose that will stand. Human planning has its place, as the preceding call to receive counsel shows, yet God’s counsel has the final word (compare 16:9).
21.explain:
“There are many plans in a man’s heart,”

People make “many plans.” The heart is full of intentions, schemes, hopes, and purposes. Planning is not wrong; the previous verse urged the son to receive counsel, which is part of planning well. The line simply observes how many and varied human plans are, and how they shift and change.

“Nevertheless the LORD’s counsel—that will stand.”

“Nevertheless” sets all those plans against one thing: “the LORD’s counsel.” His purpose “will stand.” Human plans may change, fail, or fall apart, but God’s purpose holds firm and comes to pass. The dash in the NKJV gives emphasis: that, and that alone, will stand. This restates the teaching of 16:1–9, where “A man’s heart plans his way, But the LORD directs his steps” (16:9). For those who trust Him, this is a comfort rather than a threat. Their plans rest in the hands of a God whose counsel is good and who brings His purposes to completion. The LORD Himself says, “My counsel shall stand, And I will do all My pleasure” (Isaiah 46:10).

22.brief: What people long to find in a person is kindness and faithful love, and a poor man is better than a liar. As in verse 1, honest character is worth more than wealth gained or kept through falsehood.
22.explain:
“What is desired in a man is kindness,”

What do people most want to find in another person? The verse answers, “kindness.” The Hebrew word is chesed, the term for loyal, faithful love, the steady goodness that keeps its commitments. More than money or influence, people long for someone who will be faithful to them. This is something any person can give, rich or poor.

“And a poor man is better than a liar.”

The second line makes the comparison explicit. “A poor man is better than a liar.” A poor person who is true and loyal is worth more than someone who has more but cannot be trusted. Like 19:1, which set the poor man of integrity above the fool with twisted lips, this saying weighs character above wealth. A liar may promise much and deliver nothing, while the poor man who keeps faith gives what people truly desire. The verse does not make poverty a virtue. It makes faithfulness the measure of a person.
22.notes: The ESV renders the word for “kindness” as “steadfast love.” The first line can also be read as saying that a man’s kindness is what makes him desirable, as the NASB and KJV take it, and the sense is close either way.

23.brief: The fear of the LORD, a right view of God, leads to life, and the one who has it rests content and is not visited by harm. The saying describes the general blessing of living in reverent trust, not a guarantee against every trouble.
23.explain:
“The fear of the LORD leads to life,”

“The fear of the LORD” is a right view of God. It means awe at His glory, majesty, and holiness, and a reverent trust that takes Him seriously. Such fear “leads to life,” the full life God intends. This reverent trust is different from ordinary fright. It gives grounds for contentment, and it brings a person into the life and security that come from God Himself.

“And he who has it will abide in satisfaction;”

The one who has the fear of the LORD “will abide in satisfaction.” The Hebrew verb behind “abide” means to lodge or spend the night. He lies down content, settled and satisfied, at rest under God’s care.

“He will not be visited with evil.”

The third line adds that “He will not be visited with evil,” meaning that harm will not come upon him as a visitation of judgment or ruin. The verse describes the general blessing of living in reverent trust. It is not a guarantee that a God-fearing person will never suffer trouble, sickness, or loss. Scripture is full of righteous people who suffered greatly. The promise is that the one who fears the LORD rests secure in Him, and that evil does not have the final word over his life.

24.brief: The lazy man buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth. With biting humor, the proverb shows a laziness so complete that he will not finish even the task of feeding himself.
24.explain:
“A lazy man buries his hand in the bowl,”

The picture is comic and pointed. The lazy man reaches into the bowl of food set before him, and his hand goes in. That much he manages.

“And will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.”

But then he stops. He “will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.” His hand rests in the food, and he cannot be bothered to lift it. The humor is biting: he has food right in front of him, within reach, already in his hand, and still he will not finish the simple task of feeding himself. The proverb shows a laziness so complete that it will not even take what is already provided. The failure lies in the last small step, and what he lacks is willingness, not ability or opportunity. This is a picture of settled unwillingness, not a description of those who are weak or ill. Proverbs repeats the picture with a variation in 26:15.
24.notes:
The saying is repeated with a different second line in 26:15: “It wearies him to bring it back to his mouth” (26:15).

The KJV reads ‘hideth his hand in his bosom,’ while modern versions, like the NKJV, read the Hebrew word as a bowl or dish, its usual meaning.

25.brief: When a scoffer is punished, the simple watch and learn to be careful, but a person of understanding needs only a rebuke to grow in knowledge. The scoffer himself may not change, yet discipline still teaches the onlooker, while the wise learn from a word.
25.explain:
“Strike a scoffer, and the simple will become wary;”

A “scoffer” is the person who mocks correction and will not be taught. His problem lies in his will. If he is struck, punished publicly for his wrongdoing, he himself may not change, but “the simple will become wary.” The simple, the uncommitted and easily led, see what happens to the scoffer and learn caution. The scoffer’s correction becomes a lesson for others. The Hebrew verb behind “become wary” means to become shrewd or prudent, and it is related to the word for prudence, which the book promises to give “to the simple” (1:4).

“Rebuke one who has understanding, and he will discern knowledge.”

The second line describes the person of understanding. He does not need to be struck. A “rebuke,” a word of correction, is enough, and “he will discern knowledge,” growing in understanding from it. The verse shows three kinds of people and how correction reaches each: the scoffer, who needs blows and may still not learn; the simple, who learn by watching; and the wise, who learn from a word. Correction is meant to teach and turn people toward what is right. The question the verse leaves is how much it takes to reach a person, and the wise are those whom a word can reach. The verse describes the use of correction in public justice; it gives no license for harshness, and the goal is learning, not humiliation.

26.brief: A son who mistreats his father and drives away his mother brings shame and disgrace. Turning on the parents who raised him is a deep betrayal that dishonors the whole family.
26.explain:
“He who mistreats his father and chases away his mother”

The verbs here are violent. The Hebrew verb behind “mistreat” means to assault, plunder, or devastate, so to mistreat his father is to treat him with violence or rob him, and the son who “chases away” his mother drives her out of her home. This is not a son who disagrees with his parents. He turns his strength against the very people who gave him life and raised him, and he does it when they are often weaker and dependent on him. The law commanded, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12), and this son does the opposite.

“Is a son who causes shame and brings reproach.”

Such a son “causes shame and brings reproach.” He disgraces himself and his whole family. The phrase “a son who causes shame” appeared in 17:2 and 10:5; here it reaches its strongest application. Honoring parents is measured by how a son treats them when they are vulnerable. The verse pictures a deep betrayal. It also reminds wronged parents that God sees what has been done to them.

27.brief: The father warns his son that if he stops listening to instruction, he will drift away from the words of knowledge. Wisdom is kept by continued listening, and the moment a person stops, he begins to stray.
27.explain:
“Cease listening to instruction, my son,”

In the middle of a chapter of sayings about “a man,” “the fool,” and “the poor,” the father suddenly speaks directly: “my son.” His words come with an ironic edge. “Cease listening to instruction,” he says, as if giving a command, but the next line shows what will happen if the son does. The irony is meant to warn, not to permit.

“And you will stray from the words of knowledge.”

The result of ceasing to listen is that “you will stray from the words of knowledge.” No dramatic rebellion is described. The son simply stops listening, and then he wanders. Drift begins there. Wisdom is kept by continued listening, and the moment a person stops hearing instruction, he begins to stray from what he once knew. The verse is a loving warning from a father who wants his son to keep listening.
27.notes: The KJV reads the verse quite differently: ‘Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge,’ making it a warning against false teaching. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and NIV read it as a warning about what happens when a son stops listening to instruction.

28.brief: Contempt for justice marks the worthless witness, and the mouth of the wicked gulps down evil as if it were food. The corrupt witness treats the court as a joke, while the wicked take in wrongdoing as eagerly as a hungry man eats.
28.explain:
“A disreputable witness scorns justice,”

A “disreputable witness” is a worthless, corrupt witness, one who will say whatever serves his purpose. He “scorns justice,” treating the court and its search for truth with contempt. To him, a trial is a joke and his testimony is a tool. The false witness of the chapter’s earlier warnings in 19:5 and 19:9 returns here.

“And the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.”

The second line pictures the wicked eating evil. His “mouth” “devours iniquity,” swallowing it greedily as if it were food. What troubles the conscience of others has become his appetite. A person who keeps feeding on wrongdoing comes to crave it. The witness who mocks justice and the wicked who gulp down evil belong together: both have lost any taste for what is right.
28.notes:
The Hebrew phrase behind “disreputable witness” is literally ‘a witness of Belial,’ as the KJV margin notes. Belial means worthlessness, and the expression describes a worthless or wicked person, one whose testimony cannot be trusted.

The Hebrew verb behind “devours” means to swallow or gulp down, and the ESV keeps “devours” while the YLT reads ‘swalloweth.’ The NASB and AMP read the second line ‘spreads iniquity,’ taking the verb in a different sense.

29.brief: Judgments stand ready for scoffers, and beatings for the backs of fools. Those who laugh at correction will meet it in harder form, a fitting close to a section framed by the scoffer (verse 25).
29.explain:
“Judgments are prepared for scoffers,”

The chapter ends with the scoffer, who appeared in 19:25. “Judgments are prepared” for him. They stand ready, already in place, waiting. The scoffer laughs at correction and refuses every gentler means of being taught. What remains for him is judgment.

“And beatings for the backs of fools.”

The second line repeats the thought with the image of “beatings for the backs of fools,” the stripes of punishment. Those who will not learn from a word will meet correction in harder form. The verse is a sober warning. God offers instruction, counsel, and rebuke first; refusing them all leaves only judgment. It also gives no license for cruelty. It states the consequence that awaits those who scorn every word of correction, and it closes the chapter by returning to the scoffer struck in 19:25.
